1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.c3.name: Italian Game: Classical Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.c3.background: Gioachino Greco consistently met 3...Bc5 with 4.c3, at a time when other players tended to play 4.O-O.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.c3 Nf6.name: Italian Game: Classical Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.c3 Nf6.strategy: The natural reply: develops a piece, attacks e4 and prepares to castle. With the c-pawn on c3, White's b1-knight has no square to defend e4, so White must either defend it another way or strike in the centre at once.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.c3 Qe7.name: Italian Game: Classical Variation, Closed Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.c3 Qe7.background: The move 4...Qe7 first appears in the Göttingen manuscript of about 1500, and it has always been less popular than 4...Nf6.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.c3 Qe7.strategy: Props up e5 with the queen so the centre holds, but it is a passive set-up: the queen may be misplaced on the e-file, and White can still take a full pawn centre and the space it controls.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.c3 d6.strategy: Defends e5 with a pawn and prepares to develop, but it is passive: White builds a broad pawn centre at once. Black's pieces are reasonably developed in return, and the position stays solid, if a little cramped.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.c3 d6 5.d4.strategy: Takes the centre and punishes the passive set-up: the pawn attacks both e5 and the bishop on c5. White aims for a broad pawn centre and the space it controls, and Black has to decide how to meet it.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.c3 d6 5.O-.strategy: Castles first and keeps the central strike in reserve. Black's passive set-up could be punished at once, and the extra move lets Black develop freely.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.c3 d6 5.d3.strategy: Supports the e4 pawn and prepares to castle: a slow, solid set-up that gives up the chance to take the whole centre. The game becomes a manoeuvring one in which Black's solid set-up is no longer under pressure.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.c3 d6 5.d4.strategy: Trades the e-pawn for the d-pawn. The recapture hits the bishop again, so Black accepts that White gets a strong centre and in exchange has a sound structure and a quick development.
Steps out of the pawn's reach but leaves the e5 pawn to be taken. Black can win it back with accurate play, so the move is sound, but it hands White the choice of how to play the centre.
Takes the d4 pawn with the bishop, but White recaptures with the c-pawn and has won a bishop for a pawn. Black gives away the piece that pressures the centre and gets nothing for it.

Recaptures and builds the pawn pair on d4 and e4, attacking the bishop again with gain of time. Black has to give ground in the centre once more, but the big centre needs support, and Black is well developed.

Recaptures with the knight instead of the pawn. It wins the pawn back at once, but gives Black simple trades and does not build the big centre; White keeps the structure simple and the game roughly level.

Lines up the queen and bishop against f7, so Black must defend before doing anything else. White keeps the option of recapturing on d4, but delays it, and the pawn on d4 gives Black a central foothold in the meantime.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.c3 d6 5.d4.name: Italian Game: Classical Variation, La Bourdonnais Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.c3 d6 5.d4.strategy: Retreats out of reach of the pawns while keeping the bishop on the diagonal that eyes d4 and f2. Black accepts White's big centre but has developed reasonably and aims to undermine it rather than hold it.

Checks to trade off the bishop and so relieve the pressure of White's centre, but 7.Nc3 simply blocks and keeps the big centre. If Black trades on c3, bxc3 builds an even broader one, and Black has given up its most active piece for little.
Takes the pawn but loses material: White recaptures with the knight and, after the exchanges, has won a piece for a pawn. The bishop was the piece that gave Black counterplay against the centre.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.c3 Nf6 5.d.name: Italian Game: Classical Variation, Giuoco Pianissimo
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.c3 Nf6 5.d.background: Already a frequent sideline for centuries, it became the main line in the late 20th century. John Nunn and Anatoly Karpov took it up in the 1980s, and Karpov played it in the 1981 World Championship match.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.c3 Nf6 5.d.strategy: Supports e4 and keeps the centre closed, delaying d4 until the pieces are ready. A patient plan: White develops the pieces to their best squares first and accepts a slow, manoeuvring game with little risk and few early chances for either side.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.c3 Nf6 5.d.name: Italian Game: Classical Variation, Centre Attack
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.c3 Nf6 5.d.background: Gioachino Greco developed the main line that begins here in the early 17th century, and 5.d4 stayed the main line for centuries. In the 20th century 5.d3 became the more common move.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.c3 Nf6 5.d.strategy: Strikes at the centre at once: the pawn attacks the bishop, and Black must take it or surrender the centre. The game that follows is open and sharp, with White's central pawns against Black's quick development.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.c3 Nf6 5.b.name: Italian Game: Bird's Attack
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.c3 Nf6 5.b.strategy: Attacks the bishop with a pawn to gain space on the queenside and keep chasing it. The c3 pawn covers it, so taking it costs Black a bishop for two pawns, but the pawn moves cost time while Black develops and the centre stays unbuilt.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.c3 Nf6 5.d.name: Italian Game: Classical Variation, Giuoco Pianissimo
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.c3 Nf6 5.d.strategy: Mirrors White's set-up: it defends e5 solidly and prepares to develop the c8 bishop. Black keeps the centre closed and concedes nothing, and the game becomes a slow manoeuvre with chances for both sides.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.c3 Nf6 5.d.name: Italian Game: Classical Variation, Giuoco Pianissimo, with a6
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.c3 Nf6 5.d.strategy: Makes room in advance: it takes b5 from White's bishop and frees a7 as a retreat square for the bishop on c5. The game often reaches the same structures as the main line, but Black has a useful queenside move in hand.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.c3 Nf6 5.d.name: Italian Game: Classical Variation, with d5
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.c3 Nf6 5.d.strategy: Strikes at the centre at once rather than waiting, hitting both e4 and the bishop on c4. It is playable, but it simplifies the centre early and leaves e5 as a target, so Black gains activity at the price of structure.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.c3 Nf6 5.d.name: Italian Game: Classical Variation, Giuoco Pianissimo
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.c3 Nf6 5.d.strategy: Gets the king to safety first and keeps every central plan open. A typical patient move in a slow manoeuvring game, where neither side hurries to commit.
Brings the b1 knight into play and adds a defender to e4, which relieves the d3 pawn. White keeps a flexible, patient game and opens the centre only when the pieces stand well.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.c3 Nf6 5.d.name: Italian Game: Classical Variation, Giuoco Pianissimo, Albin Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.c3 Nf6 5.d.strategy: Attacks the bishop at once to win queenside space and gain a tempo. Sharper than the quiet main plan, but the pawn advance loosens the queenside while the bishop finds a good square on b6.

Puts the king in safety before the centre can open. Nothing is gained by waiting: the centre is closed, White has no quick attack, and Black keeps every option for the bishop and the queenside pawns. A patient manoeuvring game follows, with both sides preparing a central break.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.c3 Nf6 5.d.name: Italian Game: Classical Variation, Giuoco Pianissimo, with a6
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.c3 Nf6 5.d.strategy: Takes b5 away from the white bishop, where it would pin the knight against the king, and prepares a retreat square on a7 for the bishop when White tries to chase it with b4 or d4. A useful waiting move that leaves Black flexible about castling.

Challenges the bishop that eyes f7. If White takes, the f-pawn recaptures: Black gets a half-open f-file and a grip on d5 and f5 in return for doubled pawns. If the bishop retreats, Black has developed with tempo and keeps a solid, flexible position.

Takes g5 away from White's knight and from the bishop that is still shut in on c1, so White gets no pressure on f6 or f7 from that square. A useful but slow precaution that loosens the kingside slightly and says little about the centre; Black can still castle either way.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.c3 Nf6 5.d.name: Italian Game: Classical Variation, Giuoco Pianissimo
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.c3 Nf6 5.d.strategy: The simplest plan: Black finishes kingside development and takes the king out of the centre while the position is still closed. White needs several more moves to prepare a central break, and Black meets it from a safe position.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.c3 Nf6 5.d.name: Italian Game: Classical Variation, Giuoco Pianissimo
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.c3 Nf6 5.d.strategy: Stops White from gaining space with b4 and so from chasing the bishop on c5 with a pawn. The cost is the b5 square: the white bishop can now come there to pin the knight without being asked a question. Black takes a firm stand on the queenside.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.c3 Nf6 5.d.name: Italian Game: Classical Variation, Giuoco Pianissimo
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.c3 Nf6 5.d.strategy: Stops the bishop from jumping to b5 to pin the knight, and gives the bishop on c5 the a7 square if White starts chasing it. Black keeps the question of when to castle open and waits to see which plan White chooses.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.c3 Nf6 5.d.name: Italian Game: Classical Variation, Giuoco Pianissimo
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.c3 Nf6 5.d.strategy: Moves the bishop out of reach of b4 and d4 while it keeps its eye on f2. It is playable, but on b6 the bishop can be harassed again by a queenside pawn advance, so Black may end up retreating further for nothing in return.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.c3 Nf6 5.d.name: Italian Game: Classical Variation, Giuoco Pianissimo, with h6
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.c3 Nf6 5.d.strategy: Asks the white bishop what it wants before it reaches g5: the pawn takes the square away, so the knight on f6 cannot be pinned against the queen. A sensible precaution, but it spends a tempo on the kingside and lets White regroup freely.

Removes the pawn that attacks both the bishop and the e5-pawn, and takes the fight to the centre. White will rebuild it with tempo on the bishop, so Black accepts a sharp, open game in which the central pawns decide who has the initiative.
Retreats the bishop but leaves the e5-pawn to be taken: dxe5 attacks the knight, and the pawn can be won back only with ...Nxe4, a knight then exposed to Bd5 or Qd5. White's centre goes unchallenged.
Steps back to a passive square and gives White a free hand in the centre: dxe5 hits the knight with a pawn and keeps a pawn in the middle. Black has nothing to show for the lost time.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.c3 Nf6 5.d.name: Italian Game: Classical Variation, Greco Gambit, Traditional Line
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.c3 Nf6 5.d.background: The old main line of the Giuoco Piano, developed by Gioachino Greco in the early 17th century.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.c3 Nf6 5.d.strategy: Rebuilds the broad pawn centre and attacks the bishop with tempo. White gets space and an open game; the price is that the bishop's check on b4 interrupts the build-up and the e4-pawn must be defended against the knight on f6.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.c3 Nf6 5.d.name: Italian Game: Classical Variation, Greco Gambit, Modern Line
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.c3 Nf6 5.d.background: A line favoured by Evgeny Sveshnikov, which has seen a surge in popularity in the early 21st century.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.c3 Nf6 5.d.strategy: Drives the knight away at once and gains space, leaving the recapture on d4 for later. White gets the initiative only if Black fails to strike back in the centre immediately; if it does, White keeps more space and Black has active pieces.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.c3 Nf6 5.d.name: Italian Game: Classical Variation, Greco Gambit, Dubov Italian
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.c3 Nf6 5.d.background: A gambit advocated by Daniil Dubov. In the 21st century it has emerged as a frequent alternative to 6.e5 and 6.cxd4.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.c3 Nf6 5.d.strategy: A gambit: White does not recapture, but attacks the bishop with the b-pawn and threatens to chase the knight with b5. It aims for quick development and open lines in return for a pawn. Sharp, and Black must take care not to fall behind in development.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.c3 Nf6 5.d.name: Italian Game: Scotch Gambit, Walbrodt-Baird Gambit
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.c3 Nf6 5.d.background: A rarely seen gambit that was more popular in the era of Romantic chess.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.c3 Nf6 5.d.strategy: A gambit: White castles without recapturing and lets Black take e4 as well. If Black does and White then recaptures in the centre, White is a pawn down for open lines and a lead in development; the play is level, but it asks for sharp knowledge when simply recapturing is easier.

Saves the bishop with check, so White must react before it can attend to e4, which the knight attacks. Retreating to b6 instead lets White push e5 and drive the knight away with a gain of space, which is why the check is the standard way to meet the recapture.

Keeps the bishop on its diagonal but lets White push e5 at once, hitting the knight and gaining space. White's pawns on d4 and e5 then take over the centre, and the check that would have disturbed White has not been played.
Withdraws the bishop to a passive square and lets White play e5 with tempo on the knight. White's two central pawns gain space, and Black has nothing to show for giving up the active check.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.c3 Nf6 5.d.name: Italian Game: Classical Variation, Greco Gambit, Modern Line
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.c3 Nf6 5.d.strategy: Strikes back in the centre at once: the pawn attacks the bishop, so White has to deal with that before anything else. The knight reaches a strong square on e4, Black's pieces become active, and White keeps more space. The only good answer to the push.

Runs the knight forward and into a trap: the bishop lands on d5 and the knight has no safe retreat. Black must prop it up with the f-pawn, which weakens the king's side, or sacrifice it for a speculative attack. White keeps the better chances either way.
Hits e5 and h2, but the knight stands badly: cxd4 recaptures and attacks the bishop with a pawn at the same time. White then dominates the centre while Black's knight is far from the action.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.c3 Qe7 5.d.strategy: Strikes in the centre at once: the pawn attacks the bishop and the e5-pawn, which Black's queen move was meant to hold. White gets a bigger centre and the more comfortable game, while the queen stands a little awkwardly in front of the king.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.c3 Qe7 5.O.strategy: Gets the king safe and keeps the central push in reserve, so nothing is committed yet. The queen on e7 holds e5 only while it stays there, and White can still prepare the break d4 with every piece developed.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.c3 Qe7 5.d.strategy: A quiet alternative that supports e4 and frees the c1-bishop. It gives up the immediate central break and lets Black finish development behind the solid e5-pawn, so a slow manoeuvring game follows with few chances for either side to press.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.c3 Qe7 5.d.name: Italian Game: Classical Variation, Centre Holding Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.c3 Qe7 5.d.strategy: Retreats the bishop out of the pawn's reach while it keeps its eye on f2, and holds e5 with queen and knight. Black has a compact but passive position: the e5-pawn is solid, but White has more room to move.

Takes the pawn, and the queen now looks down the open file at e4, but 6.cxd4 hits the bishop at once and gives White a central pawn pair with tempo. Black has surrendered the centre and must spend time on the bishop.
Keeps the bishop out of reach of the pawn and e5 defended, but it blocks Black's own d-pawn and leaves a passive, cramped set-up. White keeps the bigger centre and can open the game when it is ready.
Castles first and keeps the tension in the centre, so White decides when to resolve it. The bigger centre gives White a slight edge, and Black's pieces stay tied to the defence of the e5-pawn.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.c3 Qe7 5.d.name: Italian Game: Classical Variation, Mestel Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.c3 Qe7 5.d.strategy: Attacks the queen along the diagonal and forces Black to settle the pin at once. Blocking with the f-pawn weakens the king's cover; blocking with the knight lets White pin it. White gains time because Black has to respond.

Gains space and a tempo by forcing the knight back, but gives up the pressure on e5: the centre closes, and Black can regroup the knight and play against the advanced pawn. It trades flexibility for room and leads to a slow game.

Retreats the knight rather than leaving it to be taken, and keeps it in play from the back rank. White has gained space and a tempo, but the pawn on d5 has also released the pressure on e5, so Black is cramped rather than worse.
Steps back to d8, where the knight guards f7 and b7 and stays clear of the d5 pawn. Black gives up space and accepts a passive set-up, but the e5 pawn stays solid and nothing is lost.

Attacks the bishop, but the knight lands on the rim with no way back: c6 is covered by the d5 pawn, b3 by the a2 pawn, c4 by the bishop, and b7 holds Black's own pawn. White retreats with tempo and then hunts the stranded knight.

Adds a pawn to the defence of e5, so the queen is no longer needed there, and opens the diagonal for the c8-bishop. Black accepts less space for a compact structure that White cannot easily break; the game becomes a slow fight for the centre.

Develops with an attack on e4 and prepares castling, but does nothing yet about the centre: White can open it with dxe5, hitting the knight with a pawn. A natural move that leaves Black to calculate where d6 would have kept things simple.

Takes b5 from the white pieces and gives the bishop a retreat on a7 if White tries to harass it. A flexible waiting move, but it spends a tempo on the queenside while the centre remains White's to shape.
